**Solution.**

Let $c=f(0)$. We first show $c=0$.

- Setting $x=y=0$: $f(2c)=0$.
- Setting $y=0$: $f(f(x)+c)=x\,f(x)$ for all $x$. $\quad(1)$
- In $(1)$ take $x=2c$ (which is a zero of $f$): $f(f(2c)+c)=f(c)=(2c)f(2c)=0$. Hence $f(c)=0$.
- Now take $x=y=c$ in the original equation:
$$f(f(c)+f(c))=f(0)=c,\qquad (c+c)f(c+c)=(2c)f(2c)=0.$$
So $c=0$.

Thus $f(0)=0$, and $(1)$ becomes
$$f(f(x))=x\,f(x)\quad\text{for all }x. \tag{2}$$
The original equation is
$$f(f(x)+f(y))=(x+y)f(x+y). \tag{3}$$
Applying $(2)$ with $x+y$ in place of $x$ gives $f(f(x+y))=(x+y)f(x+y)$, which combined with $(3)$ yields
$$f(f(x)+f(y))=f(f(x+y))\quad\text{for all }x,y. \tag{4}$$

**Injectivity on nonzero fibers.** If $f(u)=f(v)\neq 0$, then by $(2)$,
$$u\,f(u)=f(f(u))=f(f(v))=v\,f(v)=v\,f(u),$$
so $(u-v)f(u)=0$, and since $f(u)\neq 0$, we get $u=v$. $\tag{I}$

**Additivity where the sum is nonzero-valued.** If $(x+y)f(x+y)\neq 0$, then by $(4)$,
$$f(f(x)+f(y))=f(f(x+y))=(x+y)f(x+y)\neq 0.$$
Both inputs $f(x)+f(y)$ and $f(x+y)$ are mapped by $f$ to the same **nonzero** value, so by $(I)$,
$$f(x)+f(y)=f(x+y)\quad\text{whenever }(x+y)f(x+y)\neq 0. \tag{J}$$

Now split into two cases.

**Case A: $f$ has a nonzero zero.** Let $z\neq 0$ with $f(z)=0$. Substitute $x=z$ into $(3)$:
$$f(f(z)+f(y))=f(f(y))=y\,f(y)\quad[\text{by }(2)],$$
while the right-hand side equals $(z+y)f(z+y)$. Hence
$$(z+y)f(z+y)=y\,f(y)\quad\text{for all }y. \tag{5}$$
Equivalently, $g(t):=t\,f(t)$ is $z$-periodic: $g(t+z)=g(t)$.

If $f$ were not identically zero, pick $a$ with $f(a)=b\neq 0$. Then $a\neq 0$ (since $f(0)=0$). From $(5)$ with $y=a$:
$$(z+a)f(z+a)=a\,f(a)=ab\neq 0.$$
So $(a+z)f(a+z)\neq 0$, and $(J)$ applies with $(x,y)=(a,z)$:
$$f(a)+f(z)=f(a+z)\;\Longrightarrow\;b+0=b\;\Longrightarrow\;f(a+z)=b.$$
But $f(a)=b\neq 0$ as well, so by $(I)$, $a+z=a$, giving $z=0$ — contradiction. Therefore in Case A, $f\equiv 0$.

**Case B: $f$ has no nonzero zero**, i.e. $f(x)=0\Rightarrow x=0$. Then $f$ is injective: if $f(u)=f(v)=r$, then either $r\neq 0$ (use $(I)$) or $r=0$ (then $u=v=0$). By $(4)$ and injectivity,
$$f(x)+f(y)=f(x+y)\quad\text{for all }x,y,$$
so $f$ is additive. Using additivity and $(2)$,
$$f(f(x)+f(y))=f(f(x))+f(f(y))=x\,f(x)+y\,f(y).$$
But by $(3)$ and additivity this also equals
$$(x+y)f(x+y)=(x+y)\bigl(f(x)+f(y)\bigr).$$
Equating: $x\,f(x)+y\,f(y)=(x+y)f(x)+(x+y)f(y)$, hence
$$y\,f(x)+x\,f(y)=0\quad\text{for all }x,y.$$
Setting $y=1$: $f(x)=-x\,f(1)$, i.e. $f(x)=kx$ with $k=-f(1)$. Substituting into $(3)$:
$$k^{2}(x+y)=k(x+y)^{2}\quad\text{for all }x,y,$$
which forces $k=0$, so $f\equiv 0$. But $f\equiv 0$ has every real number as a zero, contradicting the Case B hypothesis. So Case B is impossible.

Both cases force $f\equiv 0$. Finally, $f\equiv 0$ indeed satisfies the equation: $f(f(x)+f(y))=f(0)=0=(x+y)\cdot 0$.

$$\boxed{f(x)\equiv 0}$$
